newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Bombs hit Algiers before poll, kill 7, wound 77.
newsitem.headline: Bombs hit Algiers before poll, kill 7, wound 77.

text.p: Two bombs exploded in buses in the heart of Algiers on Sunday, killing seven people, wounding 77 and bringing fear to the crowded capital just days before a general election, witnesses and officials said.
The election, due on Thursday, is meant to end over five years of bloodshed, including countless bombings.
Witnesses said one bomb ripped through a crowded bus just before it was to leave Martyrs' Square in the heart of the city to take workers home around 4 p.m. (1500 GMT).
"It was full of workers heading home and the bomb went off just before it left the bus station," one witness said.
Police quickly ringed the area as ambulances, sirens screaming, raced to and from the scene, bathed in bright sunlight.
"The bus was totally destroyed, burnt out," one witness said.
Security forces said the attack which they termed a "criminal act" -- official shorthand for attacks by Moslem fundamentalists -- had killed six people, including a baby, and wounded 48.

Less than an hour after the first explosion, a hand-made bomb went off inside a bus in Gharmoul Street, in another part of the city centre. Security forces said it killed one person and wounded 29, four of them seriously.
The street houses the headquarters of the civil protection service, responsible for rescue work in such attacks. The blast was heard 1.5 km (One mile) away by guests in the Aurassi Hotel.

Bombs have killed hundreds of people and wounded thousands in the conflict between Moslem rebels and security forces, and early this year Algiers city authorities brought in draconian parking measures to try to thwart car bombs.

More than 200,000 troops and security forces are expected to be deployed nationwide for Thursday's parliamentary election to protect the nearly 18 million registered voters. But residents said there were few obvious signs so far of extra security in the capital.
There have been fears of increasing violence in the runup to Thursday's election which Algerian authorities hope will help end the years of bloodshed they blame on Moslem fundamentalists.
Algeria has been without a parliament since the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a commanding first round lead.

Violence erupted shortly afterwards and about 60,000 people have been killed. A series of massacres in isolated villages, with scores of people including children having their throats cut, have marked the runup to the election campaigning.
On Saturday, a bomb exploded in an Algiers cinema. Officials said five people were wounded, two seriously. An Algerian newspaper on Sunday put the toll at one dead and 24 wounded.
